record_type_quote:
In the ﬁrst part of the paper, we replicate past work, showing that trends
in the demand for redistribution among Americans has been largely ﬂat
or perhaps slightly negative over the last four decades. We show that this
result is robust across different redistributive questions as well as dif-
ferent data sets.

targets.authors: Kuziemko, Ilyana, Michael I. Norton, Emmanuel Saez, and Stefanie Stantcheva.
targets.title: How Elastic Are Preferences for Redistribution? Evidence from Randomized Survey Experiments.
targets.evidence_quote:
In reality, demand for
income redistribution in the United States has remained ﬂat by some mea-
sures and decreased according to others (see Kuziemko and others 2013),
as we document later in this paper.

Across the four measures, we are able
to replicate the ﬁnding of previous literature showing no increase in sup-
port for redistribution over this period of increased inequality.
targets.outcome_computational_quote:
To ensure that our heterogeneous patterns
are not driven by data or coding differences between our paper and previ-
ous work, we ﬁrst demonstrate that we can replicate the earlier ﬁnding of
ﬂat aggregate demand using our survey measures.
targets.outcome_robustness_quote:
Across the four measures, we are able
to replicate the ﬁnding of previous literature showing no increase in sup-
port for redistribution over this period of increased inequality.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The earlier flat aggregate trend survives alternative measures and survey datasets. Exact original numerical estimates are not the object of the analysis.

targets.title: Inequality, Public Opinion and Redistribution.
targets.evidence_quote:
Beyond the United States, citizens of
other countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Devel-
opment (OECD) that have seen rising income inequality generally have not
exhibited greater demand for redistribution (Kenworthy and McCall 2008).

Across the four measures, we are able
to replicate the ﬁnding of previous literature showing no increase in sup-
port for redistribution over this period of increased inequality.

reasoning: Re-analysis of existing GSS/ANES survey series checks previously reported aggregate trends with alternative questions and time windows. Treated as reproduction because the historical survey observations are reused, although additional survey series and waves also extend the analysis. The named prior empirical sources for the flat redistribution trend are Kuziemko et al. (2013) and Kenworthy and McCall (2008); theoretical models and correlates of conservatism are not targets. The reference explicitly identifies the 2013 working paper and notes its 2015 published revision.
